props.title: Miami Vice
props.initialSlug: Gritty cops go deep undercover in modern drug war

sections.content: Michael Mann's Miami Vice (2006) revolutionized digital cinematography, transforming the 80s TV show into a moody neo-noir thriller. Mann's signature high-definition digital photography creates a hypnotic atmosphere, especially in night scenes where Miami's neon bleeds into inky blacks. Like his earlier Heat (1995) and Collateral (2004), Mann explores the blurred lines between law enforcement and criminality through stylized violence and complex male relationships. The film's bold visual style influenced later digital pioneers like Zodiac (2007) and Public Enemies (2009).

sections.content: Colin Farrell and Jamie Foxx inhabit their roles as Crockett and Tubbs with a gritty intensity far removed from the original series' pastel glamour. Mann strips away 80s nostalgia for a raw examination of undercover work's psychological toll. The film's controversial digital look - simultaneously glossy and gritty - creates a unique visual language that influenced crime films like Drive (2011) and Only God Forgives (2013).

The film's technical innovations extend beyond visuals. Mann's sound design creates an immersive atmosphere where gunshots crack with devastating reality and dialogue often gets swallowed by ambient noise. This naturalistic approach influenced later films like Sicario (2015) and End of Watch (2012), where environmental authenticity trumps Hollywood polish. SUBHEAD: Digital Revolution in Crime Cinema

sections.content: Miami Vice marked a turning point in digital cinematography. Mann and cinematographer Dion Beebe pushed the Sony F900 camera to its limits, embracing digital artifacts other filmmakers avoided. This pioneering work paved the way for digital masterpieces like The Social Network (2010) and Skyfall (2012), proving digital could match or exceed film's artistic possibilities.
